findings.title: The document takes on scope that the initiative plan gives to initiatives 320, 500 and 620
findings.description:
The initiative plan (`001-initiative-plan.migratory.md`) splits the work into separate initiatives:
- **(320) Logging & Replay**
- **(500) Environment Layer**: terrain, biome, resources, seasonal state and cycle management
- **(620) Distribution & Scaling**: GPU force accumulation, variable-rate ticking, agent aggregation

This document claims all three:
- "Environment layer foundation — Terrain generation, resource placement, and the read-only query interface" (line 122).
- "Seasonal and temporal systems — seasonal cycles, resource availability shifts, day/night" (line 128).
- "Logging and replay" (line 126), plus a scope statement that lists logging infrastructure (line 21).
- About 20 lines of scaling design for 1M–4M+ entities (lines 92–112).

The slice plan (`300-slices`) has already moved away from this document. Slice 304 says "The environment layer itself — terrain, biomes, resources, seasonal logic — is owned by initiative 500". Slice 308 makes the server own the world clock only. The architecture document (dateUpdated 20260318) was never updated to match.

Seasonal ownership is also unclear inside the document itself:
- Line 72 says seasonal state advances inside the environment layer.
- Tick step 2 calls this "Environment update".
- The configuration surface (line 86) puts "seasonal cycle length" in server config.
- No section says who owns the world clock.

There is also a dependency cycle. The initiative plan says "500 depends on 300", while slice 304 depends on "(500) Environment Layer foundation slice". This document does not settle which side owns the environment interface contract.

Fix: rewrite the Scope and Anticipated Slices sections so 300 owns hosting, orchestration and the world clock, and names 320, 500 and 620 as the owners of logging/replay, environment content and scaling. State which initiative defines the environment query interface.

findings.title: The tick runs synchronously, but distribution needs async I/O, and the slow-client decision is deferred
findings.description:
Line 78 says to "run the tick synchronously, then yield to the async event loop for I/O between ticks". But tick step 5 (line 65), "State distribution — Push the committed state to connected clients", is part of the tick. In asyncio, pushing to clients means `await ws.send(...)`. With common WebSocket libraries (e.g. `websockets`), that call waits for the write buffer to drain. So either step 5 is not part of the synchronous tick, or a slow client blocks the tick loop. Line 82 depends on exactly this point but leaves the mechanism as "strategies to consider".

The design needs to state the mechanism:
- the tick publishes an immutable, serialized frame;
- each client gets its own task with a bounded queue of size 1 using latest-wins (drop stale frames);
- a write timeout leads to disconnect.

At 20 tps the budget is 50 ms. If a tick takes 40 ms, all serialization and fan-out for every client has to fit in 10 ms, and the document never accounts for that.

The stated upgrade path also has problems. It says to offload the tick "to a thread or process (NumPy releases the GIL)". That breaks "Tick as transaction" (line 39) unless the state arrays are double-buffered. Otherwise serialization in step 5 reads arrays that the next tick is already overwriting. Also, NumPy releases the GIL only inside its C kernels. Profile lookup, subset index building and spatial-hash bookkeeping in Python still hold the GIL and would compete with the event loop. Neither double-buffering nor GIL contention is mentioned.

findings.title: The document and 100-arch disagree on who owns the entity lifecycle and the state arrays
findings.description:
Line 70 says the server "assigns entity IDs, allocates space in the state arrays, and removes entities", and the behavior engine "does not manage the entity lifecycle itself". But `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:81` lists the engine interface as "tick the simulation forward, query agent state, register/remove agents". Both documents claim registration and removal.

Array ownership is also undefined. 100-arch says the engine "Returns the updated state array". This document's step 4 "State commit" means applying the result as canonical state. Neither says:
- whether the engine mutates arrays in place or returns new ones;
- who allocates the output buffers;
- whether commit is a pointer swap or a copy.

At the scale this document discusses (500K–4M entities), copying every tick is a real cost. In-place mutation would undercut "tick as transaction", because there is nothing to roll back to.

Fix: pick one owner for register/remove, and define buffer ownership (for example, server-owned double buffers that the engine writes into).

findings.title: Entity ID-to-index mapping, removal strategy and capacity overflow are not specified
Observer-driven fidelity contradicts one-way state flow and replay determinism
findings.description:
The multi-resolution design applies full simulation "to entities near observers", and aggregates disaggregate "when an observer approaches" (lines 102–104). That makes client viewpoints an input to simulation state. Which entities exist individually, and how they move, then depends on who is watching. This directly contradicts:
- "State flows outward … Nothing flows back from clients into simulation state" (line 43);
- the replay claim that "initial state plus non-deterministic inputs (entity spawns/removals, configuration changes) is sufficient" (line 90), because observer positions per tick become a replay input that is never logged.

Per-client spatial culling (line 108, slice 309) also needs a client→server message to declare the viewport. Line 68 defines the protocol as server-push only. No control channel is designed, beyond saying the protocol "should not preclude" one.

Fix: either decouple LoD from observers (base fidelity only on simulation-intrinsic criteria such as group interactions), or declare observer state an explicit, logged simulation input. Also define a minimal client→server control message type in the protocol now.

findings.title: The replay design rests on determinism that is assumed, not established
findings.description:
Line 90 says that if the tick is deterministic, logging the initial state plus inputs is enough. Several things in this design work against bit-for-bit determinism:
- **No RNG owner.** Seeds appear only for the environment (lines 72, 86). Entity spawn placement ("which profiles, how many, where") and disaggregation "spawned from the statistical model" need seeded RNG state, and the document never says who owns it or how it is logged.
- **Float order.** NumPy floating-point reduction order can vary across versions and builds, and spatial-hash iteration order affects force summation.
- **Thread offload.** The upgrade path in line 78 adds scheduling nondeterminism if anything reads state concurrently.

"Configuration changes" is listed as a replay input, but line 86 says config is loaded once at startup, and the document has no runtime configuration change path.

Fix: say whether replay must be bit-exact or only visually faithful. Name the RNG owner. For the event-only log mode, require periodic snapshots as resync points.

findings.title: What happens when a tick fails is undefined, despite "no undefined states"
"Persist state on shutdown" names a capability no component provides
The environment is called read-only, but stigmergy needs simulation writes
findings.description:
The environment is described as providing data "through a read-only query interface". The tick cycle (lines 61–66) has no step that writes back to the environment. But 100-arch's swarm archetype "respond[s] to environmental stigmergy (reinforced paths)", and the initiative plan names stigmergic trails as an environment requirement. Agents have to deposit trails, which is a write that depends on post-tick agent state.

Slice 304 already adds "Handle post-tick environment writes". The architecture should add a write-back step between commit and distribution, and say who owns that write interface.

findings.title: Overrun behavior and time semantics for the fixed timestep are ambiguous
"Support aggregation from the start" is asserted, not designed
The scaling section is oversized for a foundation architecture
The frontmatter dependency and the concept link point to a file that does not exist
findings.description:
`dependsOn: [001-concept.migratory, ...]` and the Related Work link `../project-guides/001-concept.migratory.md` (line 132) both name a file that does not exist. The concept file is `000-concept.migratory.md`; `001-` is the initiative plan.

The reverse link from `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:122` points to `200-arch.world-server-foundation.md`, which also does not exist. This document is `300-arch.worldserver-foundation.md`.
